title: The Case for a Boring Agent Graph
body_markdown:
*Written By:*[Maurice Goldberg](https://www.linkedin.com/in/goldbergmaurice/)


Let’s say you’re on call for your agent platform, working through a support ticket about your agent — let’s call it *research-agent-v2* — and the agent is returning a 500. There are calls to two different teams’ plugins in the trace, along with a subagent that you don’t remember seeing a week prior. You rerun the request to see if it fails again, but this time *research-agent-v2* builds a different graph. You’re now in the unenviable position of asking two teams to debug a failure that you can’t reliably reproduce.


At DV, we built our Agent OS platform to prevent this scenario. The problem above is that the structure of *research-agent-v2* ’s graph was decided at request time instead of release time. If the graph changes between runs, it takes far more work to compare traces and figure out which team should investigate a failure. Furthermore, rolling back the release doesn’t necessarily bring back the graph from the earlier run. For DV’s agent platform, we found that the simplest way to avoid that extra work is *not to let the graph rearrange itself in the first place* .


### One Graph, Many Assistants


DV’s Agent OS is an internal agent platform shared by the company’s product teams. Each team embeds an assistant in its own product, but every assistant runs on the same graph. At its core, the platform is a thin API layer in front of one shared runtime graph. Every assistant on the platform runs this same graph, which has two nodes, a conditional edge, and a set of middleware hooks.


The simplicity of this basic ReAct loop means that when a new product team wants to use our platform and ship their own assistant (a versioned, pinned configuration of model, prompts, plugins, and policies that runs on the shared graph), they don’t have to write an entirely new graph. Their new assistant amounts to a small repo that breaks down roughly to something like this:


```text
my-assistant/  ├── assistant.json    # display name + model  ├── system.md         # assistant-level system prompt  ├── pyproject.toml    # pinned plugin versions  └── evals/            # eval cases that gate every release   // assistant.json  {    "name": "My Assistant",    "model": "provider:model-name"  }   # pyproject.toml  dependencies = [    "plugin-domain-a==1.2.0",    "plugin-domain-b==0.4.1",  ]
```


This is the assistant’s entire surface area. The graph, loop, streaming, persistence, and gateway in front of MCP servers all stay exactly the same. The CI literally just takes that repo, deploys it as an immutable version, runs the evals against it, and only then lets you promote the assistant to be usable on the platform.


This way, plugin work can be as in-depth as the author needs, but the agent’s surface area is limited to skills, MCP tools, and evals.


### Why We Don’t Build the Graph at Runtime


Many dynamic agent patterns are getting attention in 2026, patterns like supervisor-router agents, spawn-on-demand subagents, dynamic tool loading from registries, and others. For the most part, these patterns are designed for the generic but complex use case where one team owns the whole loop and the domain is open.


For these situations, dynamic design patterns are the right fit. A generic research agent, for instance, doesn’t know what you’ll ask, and likewise, a generic coding agent can’t know ahead of time which subagents should be dispatched to solve a problem. For open-ended research and coding tasks, that flexibility can be useful, but in shipping our Agent OS system at DV, we had a different set of priorities:


#### Provide agents as a platform


Multiple product teams ship customer features on our runtime. When the graph reshapes itself per request, a bug in one team’s plugin can trip a path neither team owns. That blast radius is built into the design.


#### Enable complete vertical capability in the ad analytics space


DV’s domain is digital media measurement and optimization: viewability, fraud, brand suitability, attribution, and using that trusted measurement data to maximize campaign performance. The domain is complex, but we know which tasks our assistants need to support. A user of an agent platform can pre-declare its agents’ toolset because they know what the agent needs to do.


#### Make it productionizable


Support a clear ability to audit and reproduce bugs, eval gates, and a need to roll something back when it breaks. None of these properties stay stable in the same way with a graph that re-composes itself from run to run.


By definition, agent systems are already nondeterministic, but the question we kept coming back to is *where to allow that nondeterminism* . Our answer was inside skills, not in the graph itself. The graph is fixed when an assistant is released. At runtime, the model can choose tools, arguments, and responses within that structure. A plugin can still encode sequences and branching behavior, but it cannot recompose the runtime around itself.


### Debugging and Rollback


Say we picked a run from our agent system three months ago. What do we need to reconstruct this run’s starting conditions?


In a dynamic agent system, the honest answer is the input, version label, model weights as they were that day and a recording of every structural decision the LLM made: which subagent it spawned, tools it pulled and the plan it generated. Without that recording, you can’t reproduce it.


In our system at DV, the answer is intentionally simple. We just need:


1. Input
2. Assistant version
3. Thread state captured before the run


The assistant version identifies the graph and configuration used for the run, while the input and captured thread state provide the starting context. A rerun may still produce different tool calls, arguments, or responses, and external services may return different data. We’re still running the same graph with the same prompts and plugin versions.


For an on-call engineer, this removes one source of uncertainty: we know which graph, prompts, and plugin versions were in use. We still need the original trace to investigate what happened, but we don’t also have to reconstruct a graph assembled at request time.


Every deployed commit creates a new, immutable assistant version. When our host creates a thread, it records the selected assistant ID and uses that ID for subsequent requests. Changing the default version changes what the host selects for new threads; for existing threads, it keeps using the recorded ID.


This gives rollback a precise meaning. Rolling back to v2 means updating the release channel so new threads select v2. Our host continues using the assistant version recorded when each existing thread was created. We don’t currently support moving those threads between versions.


Fixes follow the same rule. We publish v3, run it through the release gates, and make it the default for new threads. Threads already on v2 remain on v2.


Each assistant version records exactly what shipped: the Git commit, the lockfile digest, and the resolved version of every plugin. Traces tell us what happened during a run. Release metadata tells us what was running.


Gradual rollout is then straightforward. When a thread is created, the rollout policy selects a version based on a cohort or percentage bucket. A thread in the 5% test group pins to v3; everyone else pins to v2. Expanding the rollout changes the choice for future threads, rather than threads that already exist.


### Trade-Offs


As you might expect, we give up some runtime flexibility. If a new use case does not fit the existing configuration surface, the platform team has to extend it. That puts the work on our schedule rather than the product team’s. We accept that extra work because it makes the platform easier to operate.


Agent OS also doesn’t currently provide an immediate cutoff for a vulnerable version. We can deprovision it, but cached configurations and runs already in progress may continue using it.


Furthermore, the small configuration surface, while meaningfully simplifying our operations, does not make onboarding effortless. Teams still need to understand skills, MCP tools, and evals well enough to ship effectively. To address this, we have repo templates, scaffolding skills, and SDLC documentation to help teams navigate their release process.


At DV, we chose a fixed graph because, today, it gives us a precise answer to a basic production question: what exactly was running? If improved tooling for dynamic graphs makes debugging and replay reliable enough, we’ll reconsider. The bet we’re making right now is that fixed graphs are the right answer for a vertical agent platform that needs to be traceable, auditable, and productionizable in 2026.
